questions.q: What is homeostasis defined as in biology?
a: The maintenance of a constant internal environment within restricted limits
The physical digestion of food in the stomach
The movement of water down a concentration gradient
The elimination of undigested food from the gut

questions.q: Which part of the brain acts as the body's thermostat, monitoring core blood temperature?
What is the normal core body temperature for humans around which homeostasis is maintained?
Which of the following physiological mechanisms occurs when core body temperature rises too high (e.g., during intense exercise)?
a: Hairs standing erect to trap air
Vasodilation of skin arterioles and increased sweating

questions.q: What is vasodilation?
a: The widening of arterioles supplying blood to skin capillaries, increasing heat loss by radiation and conduction
The narrowing of blood vessels to trap heat
The active pumping of sweat through ducts
The contraction of erector pili muscles

questions.q: How does vasoconstriction help conserve body heat when external temperatures are very cold?
a: It constricts arterioles in the skin, reducing blood flow through skin capillaries so less heat is lost to the environment
It increases metabolic heat production in limbs

questions.q: How does sweating cool down the human body?
a: Sweat contains cold chemicals that lower skin temperature
Heat from the blood is absorbed by sweat, causing it to evaporate from the skin surface and carry thermal energy away

questions.q: What is the role of shivering when the body gets too cold?
a: To increase blood flow to the skin
Involuntary rapid contraction of skeletal muscles, increasing cellular respiration and releasing thermal heat

questions.q: What is osmoregulation?
a: The control of water and ion (salt) balance in the body's fluids
The regulation of blood glucose levels

questions.q: Which organ is primarily responsible for osmoregulation and the removal of nitrogenous waste?
What hormone regulates the permeability of the kidney collecting ducts to water?
Where is ADH (Anti-Diuretic Hormone) produced and released into the bloodstream?
What happens to the release of ADH when a person is dehydrated (lacking water)?
a: ADH release increases, making kidney collecting ducts more permeable so a small volume of concentrated urine is produced
ADH release decreases, producing large volumes of dilute urine

questions.q: What happens to urine volume and concentration if a person drinks a very large volume of pure water?
a: Urine becomes highly concentrated and low in volume
ADH release decreases, collecting ducts become less permeable, and a large volume of dilute urine is produced

questions.q: Why is negative feedback crucial in homeostatic control systems?
a: It amplifies deviations away from normal until cell death occurs
It ensures that any deviation from a set normal point triggers a corrective response that brings the system back to the set point

questions.q: What role do erector pili muscles in the skin play during cold conditions in humans?
a: They flatten hair against the skin
They contract to pull skin hairs erect, trapping a layer of insulating air

questions.q: Which of the following describes the role of the skin in thermoregulation when external temperature is high?
a: Sweat glands secrete sweat, which evaporates to cool the body
Hairs stand erect to trap heat

questions.q: What is the primary source of metabolic heat within the human body during resting conditions?
a: Respiration in active internal organs like the liver and brain, and skeletal muscle tone

questions.q: Which blood vessel brings waste-laden blood to the kidney for filtration and osmoregulation?
What is the function of the loop of Henle and collecting duct in the mammalian nephron?
a: To concentrate urine and reabsorb water during osmoregulation

questions.q: What happens to skin arterioles during vasodilation in hot weather?
a: They widen (relax), increasing blood flow near the skin surface to radiate heat
They constrict tightly to stop blood flow

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes a negative feedback loop?
a: Stimulus (deviation from norm) -> Receptor -> Coordinator -> Effector -> Response (reverses deviation back to norm)

questions.q: What is the main danger if human core body temperature rises excessively (above 40 degrees Celsius)?
a: Denaturation of vital body enzymes due to excessive heat

questions.q: Which of the following structures acts as the effector during cooling responses like sweating?
What happens to metabolic rate when environmental temperature drops significantly in warm-blooded (endothermic) animals?
a: Metabolic rate increases to generate more internal heat
Metabolic rate converts fat into water

questions.q: Why is maintaining a constant internal body temperature important for enzyme function?
a: Enzymes work fastest at extreme boiling temperatures
Enzymes have an optimum temperature (around 37 degrees Celsius in humans); too hot causes denaturation, too cold slows kinetic energy
Temperature has no effect on enzyme activity
Enzymes require freezing conditions to stay active

questions.q: Which of the following receptors detect changes in external environmental temperature?
a: Thermoreceptors in the skin and hypothalamus

questions.q: What is the effect of decreased blood water potential (blood is too concentrated/salty) on the hypothalamus?
a: It stimulates the pituitary gland to release more ADH

questions.q: What is the primary nitrogenous waste product excreted by the kidneys during homeostasis?
Which of the following describes the body's response to a drop in external temperature?
a: Vasoconstriction, shivering, and erection of body hairs
Rapid breathing with no muscle movement

questions.q: What is the function of the renal vein leaving the kidney?
a: To carry urine to the bladder
To transport deoxygenated, filtered blood away from the kidney back toward the heart
To absorb dietary nutrients from the gut

questions.q: Why do humans flush or turn red in the face during strenuous exercise or hot weather?
a: Due to lack of oxygen in red blood cells
Due to accumulation of urea in skin
Due to vasodilation of skin arterioles bringing warm blood close to the surface to lose heat

questions.q: What is the term for animals that maintain a constant internal body temperature regardless of external surroundings?
Which of the following is NOT an example of homeostasis in humans?
a: Digesting a large meal in the stomach

questions.q: What is the role of the medulla in the kidney during urine formation?
a: To perform ultrafiltration in the glomerulus
To contain loops of Henle and collecting ducts that adjust water reabsorption

questions.q: What happens to the skin when someone is frightened or cold, causing 'goosebumps'?
a: Erector pili muscles pull hair follicles upright
